entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5363"/><div sID="gen8052" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5363"/><hi type="bold">9. unicorn--</hi>Pliny [Natural History, 8.21], mentions such an animal; its figure is found depicted in the ruins of Persepolis. The Hebrew reem conveys the idea of loftiness and power (compare Ramah; Indian, Ram; Latin, Roma). The rhinoceros was perhaps the original type of the unicorn. The Arab rim is a two-horned animal. Sometimes "unicorn" or reem is a mere poetical symbol or abstraction; but the buffalo is the animal referred to here, from the contrast to the tame ox, used in ploughing (<reference osisRef="Job.39.10">Job 39:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.39.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen8052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8053" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abide--</hi>literally, "pass the night."<div eID="gen8053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8054" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">crib--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.1.3">Is 1:3</reference>). <div eID="gen8054" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5367"/><div sID="gen8061" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5367"/><hi type="bold">13. Rather, "the wing of the ostrich hen"--</hi>literally, "the crying bird"; as the Arab name for it means "song"; referring to its night cries (<reference osisRef="Job.30.29">Job 30:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.1.8">Mi 1:8</reference>) vibrating joyously. "Is it not like the quill and feathers of the pious bird" (the stork)? [Umbreit]. The vibrating, quivering wing, serving for sail and oar at once, is characteristic of the ostrich in full course. Its white and black feathers in the wing and tail are like the stork's. But, unlike that bird, the symbol of parental love in the East, it with seeming want of natural (pious) affection deserts its young. Both birds are poetically called by descriptive, instead of their usual appellative, names. <div eID="gen8061" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5368"/><div sID="gen8062" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5368"/>14-15. Yet (unlike the stork) she "leaveth," &c. Hence called by the Arabs "the impious bird." However, the fact is, she lays her eggs with great care and hatches them, as other birds do; but in hot countries the eggs do not need so constant incubation; she therefore often leaves them and sometimes forgets the place on her return. Moreover, the outer eggs, intended for food, she feeds to her young; these eggs, lying separate in the sand, exposed to the sun, gave rise to the idea of her altogether leaving them. God describes her as she seems to man; implying, though she may seem foolishly to neglect her young, yet really she is guided by a sure instinct from God, as much as animals of instincts widely different. <div eID="gen8062" type="x-p"/>

Arab poets delight in praising the horse; yet it is not mentioned in the possessions of Job (<reference osisRef="Job.1.3">Job 1:3</reference>; 42:12).
